series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] mm: swap: move LRU insertion out of the swap cache allocator
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the insertion of a folio into the LRU (Least Recently Used) list out of the swap cache allocator. The swap cache allocator is used by zswap writeback to allocate a folio that can be freed directly once writeback completes, without being on the LRU. This change does not introduce any functional changes and only modifies the internal implementation details of the swap cache allocator.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm: swap: drop dropbehind swap cache folios on writeback completion
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the handling of drop-behind swap cache folios by freeing them immediately after writeback completion, rather than leaving them for reclaim to find later. This is done by adding two new functions: `swap_writeback_dropbehind_folio` and `swap_dropbehind_free_one_folio`, which are called when a synchronous-IO swap completes or an asynchronous block device completes writeback. The patch also updates the `remove_mapping` function to take additional parameters for tracking reclaim status and target memory cgroup. This change is necessary because synchronous-IO swaps can complete in the calling context, allowing the folio to be freed immediately, while asynchronous block devices require deferring the work to a workqueue that runs after writeback completion.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/3] mm: zswap: drop cold writeback folios via swap dropbehind
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the zswap writeback process by dropping cold folios from the LRU as soon as writeback completes, rather than leaving them on the list for reclaim to find and free later. This is done by marking the folio PG_dropbehind, which allows the swap dropbehind path to free it once writeback ends. The patch also handles synchronous-IO devices by dropping the folio inline instead of waiting for the end of writeback.

This patch addresses an issue that was previously thought to be resolved with advances in preventing such re-dirtying, and reintroduces a mechanism that was first introduced in 2008.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/4] mm/damon: defensively skip zone device folios in damon_get_folio()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the handling of zone device memory in DAMON, a kernel module for monitoring memory access patterns. The first patch adds an explicit check for zone device folios in damon_get_folio(), making the code more consistent and easier to maintain. This change is motivated by the need to abstract out these checks and make them more modular.

review_comments.author: Gregory Price
review_comments.summary: Addressed SJ's concerns by explaining that the change is motivated by the need to abstract out these checks and make them more modular, with the goal of replacing them with a single mm-wide location for these kinds of checks in the future.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Tue, Jul 28, 2026 at 05:50:36PM -0700, SJ Park wrote:
> Hi Gregory,
> 
> 
> On Tue, 28 Jul 2026 15:47:11 -0400 Gregory Price <gourry@gourry.net> wrote:
> 
> > All DAMON physical- and virtual-address operations obtain their folios
> > through damon_get_folio(). That helper already excludes ZONE_DEVICE
> > memory implicitly via pfn_to_online_page() and folio_test_lru(), but
> > this is inconsistent with other callers in mm/ which test explicitly.
> > 
> > Add an explicit folio_is_zone_device() rejection in damon_get_folio()
> > so the guarantee lives in one place and covers every caller uniformly,
> > consistent with other mm walkers that reject zone device folios.
> 
> Thank you for checking this and sharing this nice patch!
> 
> However, I'm not very sure adding a call that not really required for only
> making it looks consistent with others is the right choice.  I'm especially
> concerned if this will confuse future readers including myself.
> 
> If this is a hardening purpose, we have CONFIG_DAMON_DEBUG_SANITY for the
> purpose.  What about using it with a good comment explaining why we doing that?
> 

It's actually two fold:

  1) make zone_device more consistently handled across mm/
  2) make these checks possible to abstract out later

In the private node work - every location that we'd need to filter
folios based on private node membership is a zone_device check.

Where zone device checks are missing (like here) there's some other
implicit reason (specific to zone device) that allows it to be avoided.

I pointed out in the sashiko feedback that DAMON depends on a check
for folio->pgmap in the hotplug code.  This is all quite fragile, and
we can see that at least one patch in this series fixes an actual bug.

It seemed warranted to go audit every service and add the zone_device
checks to make it clear there's a zone device interaction - even if
presently unreachable - should some silent, implicit filter change.

The goal is to come back around and replace these with something like:

    bool folio_allows_mm_op(struct folio *folio,
                            enum node_states feature)
    {
        if (folio_is_zone_device(folio) ||
            !node_state(folio_nid(folio), feature));
    }

    - if (folio_is_zone_device(folio))
    + if (folio_allows_mm_op(folio, N_MEMORY_DAMON))

If we ever get to folios having memdesc flags beyond page flags,
this also gives us a single mm-wide location for these kinds of
checks in the future.

~Gregory

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/4] mm/huge_memory: skip zone device folios in madvise_free_huge_pmd()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the madvise_free_huge_pmd() function to skip zone device memory when resolving folios for lazyfree marking. The existing checks in the surrounding guards do not cover all cases, particularly for present zone device PMDs. By adding a check for zone device folios and bailing out if one is found, this patch ensures that such memory is not mistakenly marked as lazyfree.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/4] mm/madvise: skip zone device folios in cold/pageout PMD range
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the madvise_cold_or_pageout_pte_range function to skip zone device folios in cold/pageout PMD range, preventing them from being aged or reclaimed prematurely. The existing guards do not cover all cases of zone device memory, leading to potential issues with device-coherent THPs. By explicitly skipping ZONE_DEVICE folios, the patch addresses this problem and ensures correct behavior for these types of mappings.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/4] mm/mempolicy: skip zone device folios when queueing folios
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies three functions in the Linux kernel's memory policy module to skip zone device folios when queueing them for migration. The issue it solves is that existing checks were not sufficient to prevent zone device PMDs from being added to the migration pagelist, which could lead to incorrect behavior and unnecessary failures. The approach taken is to add explicit checks in each of the three functions (queue_folios_pmd, queue_folios_pte_range, and queue_folios_hugetlb) to skip zone device folios, mirroring the existing check in one of the functions.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series adds missing checks for ZONE_DEVICE memory in various mm walkers, ensuring that zone device folios are not lazily freed or aged prematurely. The changes aim to harden the kernel by making these checks consistent across different walkers and providing a clear indication of when zone device interactions occur.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v4 02/21] iomap: decouple simple direct I/O reads from iomap_dio_rw
series_items.patch_summary: This patch decouples simple direct I/O reads from the iomap_dio_rw function to improve performance by allowing file systems to call into a new simple path explicitly, which can be inlined and optimized by the compiler. This change is necessary because the current implementation assumes that the iterator must be advanced at the end, but the direct I/O read fast path tries to avoid this. By splitting the simple path from iomap_dio_rw, file systems are required to only call the simple path for cases they can handle, and various checks for incompatible features can be dropped.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series converts the iomap code to use an iterator model, replacing the current begin/end pair of callbacks with a single next callback. This change allows for improved performance by enabling inlining and devirtualization of the iteration loop, as well as providing more flexibility for future callers to express custom logic in the IO path. The patches are broken down into 21 steps, including refactoring existing code, adding the new next callback, converting each filesystem, removing legacy paths, and updating documentation.

review_comments.summary: The author is addressing a concern about the fallback path for filesystems that don't provide an ->iomap_next() callback, explaining that iomap_iter() will fall back to the ->iomap_begin()/->iomap_end() path. review_comments.raw_body:
Have one ->iomap_next() callback instead of ->iomap_begin() and
->iomap_end(). ->iomap_next() finishes the previous mapping if needed,
and produces the next mapping.

Collapsing to a single callback lets a performance-critical caller
inline its iteration loop and pass its ->iomap_next() function as a
compile-time constant, so the compiler can devirtualize that callback
into a direct call instead of an indirect call through a function
pointer.

iomap_iter() uses ->iomap_next() when the filesystem provides that
callback and otherwise falls back to the ->iomap_begin()/->iomap_end()
path, so filesystems can be converted one at a time.

Suggested-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Suggested-by: Matthew Wilcox (Oracle) <willy@infradead.org>
Reviewed-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Signed-off-by: Joanne Koong <joannelkoong@gmail.com>

 2 files changed, 15 insertions(+), 2 deletions(-)

diff --git a/fs/iomap/iter.c b/fs/iomap/iter.c
index 66ccb87441ab..e05574602946 100644
--- a/fs/iomap/iter.c
+++ b/fs/iomap/iter.c
@@ -107,8 +107,12 @@ int iomap_iter(struct iomap_iter *iter, const struct iomap_ops *ops)
 
 	trace_iomap_iter(iter, ops, _RET_IP_);
 
-	ret = iomap_iter_next(iter, &iter->iomap, &iter->srcmap,
-			ops->iomap_begin, ops->iomap_end);
+	if (ops->iomap_next)
+		ret = ops->iomap_next(iter, &iter->iomap, &iter->srcmap);
+	else
+		ret = iomap_iter_next(iter, &iter->iomap, &iter->srcmap,
+				ops->iomap_begin, ops->iomap_end);
+
 	iter->status = 0;
 	if (ret > 0)
 		iomap_iter_done(iter);
diff --git a/include/linux/iomap.h b/include/linux/iomap.h
index 80832edc7ec2..d203d9fe0f89 100644
--- a/include/linux/iomap.h
+++ b/include/linux/iomap.h
@@ -231,9 +231,18 @@ typedef int (*iomap_iter_begin_fn)(struct inode *inode, loff_t pos,

+/*

+		struct iomap *iomap, struct iomap *srcmap);
+
 struct iomap_ops {
 	iomap_iter_begin_fn iomap_begin;
 	iomap_iter_end_fn iomap_end;
+	iomap_iter_next_fn iomap_next;

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 04/12] mm/gup: let check_vma_flags() ignore selected VMA flags
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the check_vma_flags() function in the mm/gup.c file to allow callers to ignore specific VMA flags when checking for compatibility with gup operations. The function now takes an additional 'ignore_flags' argument, which is used to clear selected flags from the local copy of vma->vm_flags before performing checks. This change is intended to prepare for future use cases where it's necessary to reach COWed pages in VM_IO or VM_PFNMAP VMA regions without repeating flag tests.

review_comments.author: John Hubbard
review_comments.summary: Reviewer John Hubbard noted that the ignore_flags argument can alter permission, shadow-stack, and COW validation due to its interaction with various flag checks implemented through helpers, and suggested replacing it with a single-purpose internal GUP flag, FOLL_PFNMAP_COW.
review_comments.raw_body:
All callers pass zero in this patch, so there is no behavior change yet.
The problem is the interface being added.

The same local vm_flags value is used for the VM_IO/VM_PFNMAP gate,
VM_WRITE, VM_SHADOW_STACK, VM_READ, VM_MAYREAD, and is_cow_mapping().

An arbitrary mask can therefore alter permission, shadow-stack, and COW
validation. For example, masking VM_SHARED changes the result of
is_cow_mapping(), while masking VM_SHADOW_STACK removes its write
rejection. Checks implemented through helpers still read the original
vma->vm_flags, so the meaning of ignore_flags also depends on how each
check happens to be implemented.

Perhaps it is best to replace the mask with a single-purpose internal
GUP flag, such as FOLL_PFNMAP_COW, and apply it only to the
special-mapping gate:

	if (vm_flags & (VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP) &&
	    (!(gup_flags & FOLL_PFNMAP_COW) ||
	     !(vm_flags & VM_PFNMAP)))
		return -EFAULT;

This permits the later caller to examine a VM_PFNMAP mapping while
keeping VM_IO-only mappings and every other VMA check unchanged.



thanks,
-- 
John Hubbard

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 05/12] mm/gup: add get_user_page_vma() to fault in a page under a held lock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function called get_user_page_vma() to the Linux kernel's mm/gup.c file. It is designed to fault in a single page under a held lock, either the mmap lock or the per-VMA lock. The function simplifies __get_user_pages() by walking the page tables with follow_page_mask(), faults in missing pages with faultin_page(), and returns the page with a reference still held by the caller. It also includes checks for VM_IO/VM_PFNMAP VMA exceptions, userfaultfd VMA handling, and error cases where the lock is released and -EAGAIN is returned.

return -EAGAIN. I think it's still relevant for when we use mmap_lock.

returns something unexpected, shouldn't we return -EAGAIN to retry
under mmap_lock and get the definitive result?

review_comments.author: John Hubbard
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer John Hubbard noted that the get_user_page_vma() function does not handle the case where a page is already mapped in the VMA's page tables, and requested that the function check for this condition before attempting to fault in the page.

The reviewer pointed out a difference in behavior between VM_IO and VM_PFNMAP VMA types, noting that VM_IO only indicates that MM callers should not inspect the mapped pages due to side effects, whereas VM_PFNMAP identifies mappings whose COWed pages should be returned. The reviewer suggested testing for VM_PFNMAP specifically instead of treating both as exceptions.
review_comments.raw_body:
On 7/24/26 3:29 PM, Rik van Riel wrote:
...

---

This treats VM_IO and VM_PFNMAP as the same exception, but they have
different meanings. VM_IO tells MM callers not to inspect the mapped
pages because accesses can have side effects. It does not imply that
the VMA contains raw PFNs!

For example, sg_mmap() creates a VM_IO-only VMA whose fault handler
installs ordinary pages from the SCSI reserve buffer. If such a page is
already present, follow_page_mask() returns it before the pfnmap test
below is reached. Patch 6 then lets /proc/PID/mem and ptrace copy that
page directly, even though sg provides no ->access callback and the
operation fails today. Writes can also modify the buffer when the
mapping is writable. Existing ptrace authorization still applies, so
this is not a privilege bypass, but it removes the VM_IO exclusion for
a driver that did not opt in through ->access.

An untouched page in the same VMA still fails because pfnmap is also
true for VM_IO and this function refuses to fault it. The result
therefore depends on whether the target previously touched the page.
The required exception is narrower. A remap_pfn_range() VMA has both
VM_IO and VM_PFNMAP, but VM_PFNMAP is what identifies the mapping whose
COWed page should be returned. 

So if you use the FOLL_PFNMAP_COW flag suggested on patch 4, and test
only VM_PFNMAP here:

	ret = check_vma_flags(vma, gup_flags);
	if (ret)
		goto fail;
	pfnmap = vma->vm_flags & VM_PFNMAP;

Patch 6 can set FOLL_PFNMAP_COW for __access_remote_vm().
check_vma_flags() then permits VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP for that caller while
continuing to reject VM_IO-only mappings. vm_normal_page() supplies the
remaining distinction: it returns the COWed normal page and rejects the
raw PFN.

Something like that.

thanks,
-- 
John Hubbard

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 08/12] selftests/mm: cover /proc/pid/mem access to VM_PFNMAP memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds two tests to the selftests/mm/pfnmap.c file, which cover accessing VM_PFNMAP memory through /proc/pid/mem. The first test, procmem_cow_read, maps a private and writable file, writes to a copy-on-write (COW) page, and then reads it back through /proc/self/mem. The second test, procmem_pfn_read, reads a raw physical frame number (PFN) directly through vma->vm_ops->access(), which ioremaps the PFN and rejects RAM pages. series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the follow_page_mask() function in the mm/gup module to return the number of contiguous pages covered by a page, rather than a bitmask representing the enclosing huge page. The function now takes an additional 'end' argument that bounds how far the walk looks, allowing for more efficient handling of large folios and preventing unnecessary scanning. series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 11/12] mm/gup: batch contiguous PTE-mapped large folios in follow_page_mask()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the handling of PTE-mapped large folios in the Linux kernel's memory management system by batching contiguous pages together, reducing the number of page table walks required. This is achieved through a new function called `folio_pte_batch_flags()` that counts consecutive present PTEs mapping consecutive pages with uniform write bits. series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC v4 12/12] selftests/mm: add a slow-GUP content and COW test for mTHP
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new test, mthp_gup_cow_test, to the Linux kernel selftests suite. The test checks that the slow get_user_pages() path correctly handles large folios (mTHP) and copy-on-write (COW) operations. It does this by pinning a region of memory on the slow path, writing a distinct pattern to each page, and then verifying that the kernel copies back the correct contents from the pinned pages after a COW operation. The test also reports how many pages are in contiguous large-folio runs, allowing for better coverage testing of kernels without mTHP support.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch renames the function get_user_page_vma_remote() to get_user_page_lookup_vma() to improve namespace clarity and prepare for a new variant of this function that takes a VMA as an argument. The rename is done in multiple files, including arch-specific code and include files. This change does not introduce any functional changes.

review_comments.author: Rik Riel (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about check_vma_flags() rejecting VM_IO and VM_PFNMAP VMA flags, which prevents reaching COWed pages in these mappings. The author added an ignore_flags argument to check_vma_flags(), allowing callers to drop specific rejections while keeping others. This change prepares for get_user_page_vma(), which will pass VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP to reach those COWed pages.

review_comments.author: Rik Riel (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed concerns about contention on large multi-threaded workloads between readers and writers of mmap() or munmap(), which stall readers like /proc/PID/cmdline, /proc/PID/environ, or /proc/PID/mem. The author proposed using the per-VMA lock to access a remote process's memory when the access fits in one VMA, adding an unlocked variant of untagged_addr_remote() and annotating reads with READ_ONCE() and writes with WRITE_ONCE() for KCSAN-clean accesses.

review_comments.author: Rik Riel (author)
review_comments.summary: The author addressed a concern about contention on mmap_read_lock() in __access_remote_vm(), explaining that using per-VMA lock would avoid this issue and provide a modest speedup. The author confirmed they will use the per-VMA lock when an access fits within one VMA, but fall back to the mmap lock for multi-VMA accesses or other cases.
review_comments.raw_body:
__access_remote_vm() holds mmap_read_lock() for the whole transfer. On
large machines, with large multi-threaded applications, the mmap_lock
is often contended, leading to things like reads of /proc/PID/cmdline
stalling.

This results in system monitoring tools getting stuck, right when
system information would be the most helpful.

That problem can be avoided by having __access_remote_vm() access
user memory under the per-VMA lock. The old code also looks up
the VMA for every page accessed, and walks the page tables for
every page inside a large folio. Cleaning that up speeds things
up nicely.

Using code that does not include its own lock dance, and does not
look up the VMA twice results in a modest speedup.

	read size   baseline    per-VMA     throughput
	8 B          201.7 ns    170.6 ns    ~15% faster
	4 KB         495 ns      442 ns      +12% (8266 -> 9265 MB/s)
	64 KB       4115 ns     3355 ns      +23% (15927 -> 19536 MB/s)
	1 MB       75902 ns    63641 ns      +19% (13815 -> 16477 MB/s)

The multi-threaded reader-versus-writer contention that motivates the lock
is not measured.

The rest of the series builds on this to batch per-VMA GUP. Patches 9-12
have follow_page_mask() report a contiguous PTE-mapped run of a large
folio, so the slow pin_user_pages() path walks it once instead of per page.
Other paths that walk a range benefit too.

That batching pays off on PTE-mapped mTHP. With mm/gup_test.c
(PIN_LONGTERM_BENCHMARK, the slow pin_user_pages() path) on a 256 MB
MADV_HUGEPAGE region in a 4 CPU VM, median get time over 16 iterations:

	gup_test -L -m 256 -n 65536 -r 16 -t
	                      before      after
	64 kB mTHP            3140 us      412 us   (7.6x)
	2 MB THP (control)      78 us       76 us
	4 kB base (control)   3010 us     3042 us

The PMD-mapped 2 MB THP already returns in one step, so only the PTE-mapped
large folio case improves.

Reaching a page under the per-VMA lock means looking up the VMA first,
which needs to untag the remote address without the mmap lock. The untag
masks (x86 LAM, riscv pointer masking) change only while the target is
single-threaded, so a remote reader races at most one such change.

Those masks are already read locklessly elsewhere, so patches 1 and 2 add
untagged_addr_remote_unlocked() helpers with READ_ONCE()/WRITE_ONCE()
annotations. A stale read sees the old or new mask, never a torn value, and
the remote untag is best-effort.

With the VMA in hand we need one page from it under the lock the caller
already holds. get_user_pages_remote() does not fit: it hard codes the mmap
lock and re-derives the VMA internally.

Rather than reimplement GUP in yet another caller, this version follows
David Hildenbrand's v2 guidance: start from a proper GUP interface that
takes a locked VMA, not an mm, and decide which faults can resolve under
the VMA lock.

Patch 3 renames get_user_page_vma_remote() to get_user_page_lookup_vma() to
free the name. Patch 5 adds get_user_page_vma(): a simplified
__get_user_pages() that walks the tables with follow_page_mask(), faults a
missing page in with faultin_page(), and returns it with a reference and
the caller's lock still held.

Like __get_user_pages() it runs check_vma_flags(), so callers need not
pre-check the VMA.

A VM_IO or VM_PFNMAP VMA is the exception: a COWed page with a struct page
is returned normally, while a raw PFN yields -EFAULT so the caller can
reach vma->vm_ops->access(). The caller sets FOLL_VMA_LOCK when it holds
the per-VMA lock, which reaches the fault code as FAULT_FLAG_VMA_LOCK.

Anything the per-VMA lock cannot finish releases the lock and returns
-EAGAIN, so the caller retries under the mmap lock: a dropped fault, a
userfaultfd VMA (which assumes current is the faulting task), a hard error,
or ->access() memory. faultin_page() reports the retry the same way for
both lock types.

__access_remote_vm() then uses the per-VMA lock when an access fits within
one VMA, and falls back to the mmap lock for multi-VMA accesses, stack
expansion, or an -EAGAIN from get_user_page_vma().

Walking page tables under only the per-VMA lock is safe against both page
table freeing and THP collapse. munmap() frees a VMA's page tables under
the VMA write lock that our read lock excludes, so they cannot be torn down
under the walk.

THP collapse needs neither lock: it retracts a PTE page under the page
table lock and frees it by RCU.

follow_page_pte() takes that same lock through pte_offset_map_lock() and
rechecks the pmd, so it either walks an intact table or sees the collapsed
pmd and faults the page in, while RCU keeps the retracted page valid.

A COWed page in a VM_PFNMAP mapping was previously unreachable through
/proc/pid/mem because generic_access_phys() rejects ioremaps of RAM. With
get_user_page_vma() returning the struct page directly, that read now
succeeds, which the new selftests cover along with the raw PFN path.

Thanks to Suren for pointing out the need, to David for pushing me
to just rework the whole area, to Usama for reviewing the arch patches,
and Lorenzo for the changelog and cover letter cleanups.

There is a lot more work that could be done in this area, but the
patch series is big enough. More changes can come in follow up work.

__access_remote_vm() needs a single page from a VMA it has already
looked up and locked, faulting it in when necessary, under either the
mmap lock or the per-VMA lock. get_user_pages_remote() does not fit: it
hard codes the mmap lock and re-looks-up the VMA, neither of which is
wanted here.

Add get_user_page_vma(), a simplified __get_user_pages() that walks the
page tables with follow_page_mask(), faults a missing page in with
faultin_page(), and on success returns it with a reference and the
caller's lock still held. Like __get_user_pages() it runs
check_vma_flags(), so callers need not pre-check the VMA.

A VM_IO/VM_PFNMAP VMA is the exception to that check: it can still hold
COWed pages that have a struct page, so follow_page_mask() is allowed to
look for one. Memory with no struct page -- a raw PFN, or a present PFN
reported as -EEXIST -- is returned as -EFAULT, so the caller can reach it
through vma->vm_ops->access().

The caller sets FOLL_VMA_LOCK when it holds the per-VMA lock rather than
the mmap lock, which reaches the fault code as FAULT_FLAG_VMA_LOCK.

Anything that cannot complete under the per-VMA lock -- a dropped fault,
a userfaultfd VMA (uffd assumes current is the faulting task), a hard
error, or ->access() memory -- releases the lock and returns -EAGAIN,
so the caller retries under the mmap lock.

faultin_page() reports these retries as -EAGAIN for both lock types;
only the mmap caller records the dropped lock in *locked.

A VM_FAULT_ERROR decoding to no errno now returns -EFAULT instead of
BUG(), warning under CONFIG_DEBUG_VM. This relaxes the same case on the
existing __get_user_pages() path too.

review_comments.raw_body:
__access_remote_vm() reads another task's memory under the mmap lock. That
lock is contended on large multi-threaded workloads, where an mmap() or
munmap() stalls readers like /proc/PID/cmdline or process_vm_readv() even
though the target memory is resident and reachable under the per-VMA lock.

Reaching it under the per-VMA lock means looking up the VMA first, which
requires untagging the remote address without the mmap lock. riscv's
untagged_addr_remote() asserts that lock and has no unlocked variant; the
generic untagged_addr_remote_unlocked() falls back to untagged_addr(),
which masks against current->mm, not the target mm.

Add untagged_addr_remote_unlocked(), which masks @addr against the target
mm without asserting the lock, and redefine untagged_addr_remote() on top
of it so it keeps the assertion.

The mask width is mm->context.pmlen, written while a program is single
threaded, and frozen with MM_CONTEXT_LOCK_PMLEN once it spawns a second
thread.

That read need not be stable: pmlen is already read locklessly by
untagged_addr() and mm_untag_mask(), and a remote untag is best-effort.
Annotate the lockless reads with READ_ONCE() and the writes with
WRITE_ONCE(), so a reader sees one whole value and the accesses are
KCSAN-clean.

> wanted here.
>
> Add get_user_page_vma(), a simplified __get_user_pages() that walks the
> page tables with follow_page_mask(), faults a missing page in with
> faultin_page(), and on success returns it with a reference and the
> caller's lock still held. Like __get_user_pages() it runs
> check_vma_flags(), so callers need not pre-check the VMA.
>
> A VM_IO/VM_PFNMAP VMA is the exception to that check: it can still hold
> COWed pages that have a struct page, so follow_page_mask() is allowed to
> look for one. Memory with no struct page -- a raw PFN, or a present PFN
> reported as -EEXIST -- is returned as -EFAULT, so the caller can reach it
> through vma->vm_ops->access().
>
> The caller sets FOLL_VMA_LOCK when it holds the per-VMA lock rather than
> the mmap lock, which reaches the fault code as FAULT_FLAG_VMA_LOCK.

> a userfaultfd VMA (uffd assumes current is the faulting task), a hard

>

All callers pass zero in this patch, so there is no behavior change yet.
The problem is the interface being added.

The same local vm_flags value is used for the VM_IO/VM_PFNMAP gate,
VM_WRITE, VM_SHADOW_STACK, VM_READ, VM_MAYREAD, and is_cow_mapping().

An arbitrary mask can therefore alter permission, shadow-stack, and COW
validation. For example, masking VM_SHARED changes the result of
is_cow_mapping(), while masking VM_SHADOW_STACK removes its write
rejection. Checks implemented through helpers still read the original
vma->vm_flags, so the meaning of ignore_flags also depends on how each
check happens to be implemented.

Perhaps it is best to replace the mask with a single-purpose internal
GUP flag, such as FOLL_PFNMAP_COW, and apply it only to the
special-mapping gate:

	if (vm_flags & (VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP) &&
	    (!(gup_flags & FOLL_PFNMAP_COW) ||
	     !(vm_flags & VM_PFNMAP)))

keeping VM_IO-only mappings and every other VMA check unchanged.

On 7/24/26 3:29 PM, Rik van Riel wrote:
...
> +struct page *get_user_page_vma(struct vm_area_struct *vma, unsigned long addr,
...
> +	ret = check_vma_flags(vma, gup_flags, VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP);
> +	if (ret)
> +		goto fail;
> +	pfnmap = vma->vm_flags & (VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP);

This treats VM_IO and VM_PFNMAP as the same exception, but they have
different meanings. VM_IO tells MM callers not to inspect the mapped
pages because accesses can have side effects. It does not imply that
the VMA contains raw PFNs!

For example, sg_mmap() creates a VM_IO-only VMA whose fault handler
installs ordinary pages from the SCSI reserve buffer. If such a page is
already present, follow_page_mask() returns it before the pfnmap test
below is reached. Patch 6 then lets /proc/PID/mem and ptrace copy that
page directly, even though sg provides no ->access callback and the
operation fails today. Writes can also modify the buffer when the
mapping is writable. Existing ptrace authorization still applies, so
this is not a privilege bypass, but it removes the VM_IO exclusion for
a driver that did not opt in through ->access.

An untouched page in the same VMA still fails because pfnmap is also
true for VM_IO and this function refuses to fault it. The result
therefore depends on whether the target previously touched the page.
The required exception is narrower. A remap_pfn_range() VMA has both
VM_IO and VM_PFNMAP, but VM_PFNMAP is what identifies the mapping whose
COWed page should be returned. 

So if you use the FOLL_PFNMAP_COW flag suggested on patch 4, and test
only VM_PFNMAP here:

	ret = check_vma_flags(vma, gup_flags);
	if (ret)
		goto fail;
	pfnmap = vma->vm_flags & VM_PFNMAP;

Patch 6 can set FOLL_PFNMAP_COW for __access_remote_vm().
check_vma_flags() then permits VM_IO | VM_PFNMAP for that caller while
continuing to reject VM_IO-only mappings. vm_normal_page() supplies the
remaining distinction: it returns the COWed normal page and rejects the
raw PFN.

Something like that.

thanks,
-- 
John Hubbard
